title: NURS 1017 Unit 5 Case Study 5
description: 42-year-old female admitted with deep partial-thickness and circumferential full-thickness third-degree burns to her right leg and forearm, presenting with neurovascular compromise requiring emergency bedside escharotomy, followed by management of the post-burn hypermetabolic state and wound healing.

question.stem: The nurse conducts a focused neurovascular and wound assessment on Karen's burned right lower extremity. Which assessment cues indicate circumferential third-degree full-thickness burn injury with impending compartment syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.text: Right calf and foot feel cool to touch, with progressive loss of palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, confirmed faint on Doppler ultrasound
Wound surface across the right lower leg is dry, leathery, charred white and dark brown, with complete absence of sensation to pinprick (insensate)
Severe, unremitting deep ache and agonizing pain elicited upon passive dorsiflexion of the right toes
Right calf tissue feels tense, rock-hard, and woody to palpation underneath the rigid circumferential burn eschar
Bright red, moist, weeping wound on the thigh with thin-walled fluid-filled blisters that blanch briskly with extreme pain
Paresthesias and progressive numbness spreading across the right plantar and dorsal foot surfaces

question.explanation:
1. Full-Thickness (Third-Degree) Burn: Destroys the epidermis, entire dermis, and epidermal appendages into subcutaneous fat; appears dry, leathery, charred white, brown, or black, and is insensate to pinprick because dermal sensory nerve endings are incinerated.
2. Compartment Syndrome in Circumferential Burns: Circumferential full-thickness eschar cannot stretch. As massive resuscitation edema expands within the rigid fascial compartments beneath the leathery eschar, interstitial pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure (> 30 mm Hg), cutting off arterial inflow and venous outflow. Hallmark cues include: hard, woody muscle compartments; severe deep pain on passive muscle stretch; paresthesias; coolness; and loss of distal pulses (a late, critical sign of impending gangrene and muscle necrosis). Moist weeping blisters with brisk blanching describe a second-degree superficial partial-thickness burn.

question.stem: The nurse analyzes the depth of tissue destruction across Karen's wounds. For each clinical description, click to specify the corresponding burn depth classification according to American Burn Association criteria.

rows.text: Destruction limited to outermost epidermis; dry, red, painful, blanches briskly, no blisters, heals in 3 to 6 days without scarring
Epidermis and papillary dermis destroyed; moist, thin-walled weeping blisters, bright red or pale ivory, exquisite pain, blanches with pressure, heals in 7 to 21 days
Destruction through entire dermis into subcutaneous tissue; dry, hard, leathery texture, waxy-white or charred black, insensate to pinprick, requires skin grafting
Involves entire reticular dermis leaving only hair follicles; mottled waxy-white surrounded by pink, sluggish or absent blanching, less painful, often excised and grafted

question.preamble: The nurse reviews burn wound depth taxonomy prior to surgical debridement. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1620 and the Burn Classification Reference.
question.explanation:
1. First-Degree (Superficial): Involves only the epidermis (e.g., standard sunburn). Red, dry, painful, no blisters, heals in 3–6 days.
2. Second-Degree Superficial Partial-Thickness: Involves epidermis and upper (papillary) dermis. Moist, thin-walled weeping blisters, extreme pain, brisk blanching, heals in 7–21 days.
3. Second-Degree Deep Partial-Thickness: Involves the entire dermis down to reticular layers, preserving only deep hair follicles/sweat glands. Mottled waxy-white with red areas, sluggish blanching, reduced sensation, heals slowly with severe scarring unless excised and grafted early.
4. Third-Degree Full-Thickness: Involves epidermis, entire dermis, and subcutaneous fat. Dry, leathery eschar, charred black, brown, or translucent white, insensate to light touch/pinprick because nerves are destroyed, requires surgical excision and grafting.
5. Fourth-Degree: Full thickness extending into underlying fascia, muscle, tendon, or bone (common in high-voltage electrical injuries).

question.stem:
The nurse analyzes the metabolic and physiological consequences of major burn trauma during the post-resuscitation period.

Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1000 (Post-Burn Day 3) and the Wound Healing Stages Reference.
question.explanation:
1. Hypermetabolic State: Severe burns trigger the highest hypermetabolic response of any human trauma (metabolic rate can exceed 150–200% of baseline). It is mediated by a massive neuroendocrine surge of catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine), corticosteroids (cortisol), and glucagon, persisting for weeks to months.
2. Catabolism: This hormonal surge stimulates glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and massive skeletal muscle proteolysis (breakdown of muscle into alanine and glutamine to fuel hepatic gluconeogenesis), causing severe negative nitrogen balance, muscle wasting, and delayed wound healing.
3. Early Enteral Nutrition: Initiating high-protein (1.5–2.0 g/kg/day), high-calorie enteral feeding within the first 24 hours maintains splanchnic blood flow, prevents gut mucosal atrophy and bacterial translocation, blunts the hypermetabolic surge, and provides the amino acids essential for collagen synthesis across wound healing phases.

cloze.text: Following major burn trauma, the body enters a profound hypermetabolic state driven by massive release of [[drop0]] from the neuroendocrine system. This hypermetabolic stress response induces severe whole-body catabolism characterized by [[drop1]], resulting in rapid loss of lean muscle mass and impaired immune defense. To support wound healing, prevent gut mucosal atrophy, and blunt catabolism, the nurse prioritizes [[drop2]] initiated as early as possible.

tabs.title: Wound Healing Stages Reference
tabs.content:
Four Phases of Natural Wound Healing in Burns:
  • Phase 1: Hemostasis: Platelet aggregation, fibrin clot formation, provisional matrix.
  • Phase 2: Inflammation: Neutrophil and macrophage infiltration, cytokine release (VEGF, TGF-β, PDGF), clearing debris/bacteria.
  • Phase 3: Proliferation: Fibroblast migration, collagen deposition, angiogenesis, epithelialization.
  • Phase 4: Remodeling: Collagen cross-linking, matrix remodeling by MMPs, scar contracture maturation.

question.stem: The nurse is developing the multi-system rehabilitation and infection control care plan for Karen. Which nursing interventions are appropriate during the acute and rehabilitative phases of burn care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apply prescribed topical antimicrobial agents (e.g., silver sulfadiazine or mafenide acetate) to debrided burn wounds using strict aseptic technique
Enforce complete bed rest with permanent immobilization of all burned limbs for 6 weeks
Administer prescribed intravenous opioid analgesics approximately 20 to 30 minutes prior to scheduled wound debridement and dressing changes
Perform active and passive range-of-motion (ROM) exercises to all affected joints several times daily and apply custom splints in positions of functional extension to prevent joint contractures
Monitor blood glucose levels regularly, as burn-induced cortisol and catecholamine surges induce significant stress hyperglycemia and insulin resistance
Position the right knee and right ankle in comfortable, dependent, flexed positions with pillows beneath the knees at all times

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1330.
question.explanation: Appropriate nursing interventions include: (Option 4) Aggressive physical therapy, ROM exercises, and splinting in neutral or extended positions to combat the powerful forces of myofibroblast-mediated scar contractures across joints; (Option 3) Pre-medicating with analgesics before dressing changes, which are intensely painful; (Option 1) Aseptic application of topical antimicrobials (silver sulfadiazine, mafenide acetate) to suppress microbial colonization in avascular eschar; and (Option 5) Glycemic monitoring, as stress hormones cause severe insulin resistance. Positioning limbs in dependent flexion ('positions of comfort') is the primary cause of crippling permanent contractures (e.g., knee flexion contractures, foot drop); joints must be maintained in functional extension. Complete immobilization promotes deep vein thrombosis and permanent joint ankylosis.

question.stem: The nurse reviews clinical actions and wound management orders for Karen on Post-Burn Day 7 as she prepares for tangential excision and autografting. For each nursing action, click to specify whether the intervention is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Monitor donor and recipient skin graft sites postoperatively for seroma, hematoma, or infection that could compromise graft take
Elevate the right lower extremity above heart level on pillows to reduce dependent edema and facilitate venous return
Discontinue all enteral nutritional feedings 48 hours prior to surgical skin grafting to induce gastric atrophy
Assess the newly grafted right leg for complete immobilization and prevent shear forces during the first 3 to 5 days post-grafting
Perform hourly arterial blood gas punctures in the non-burned left arm
Allow open, uncleaned burn wounds to remain exposed to ambient ward air without protective dressings

question.preamble: Pre- and post-grafting clinical care management. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1600 (Post-Op Day 1 / Post-Burn Day 8).
question.explanation:
1. Indicated: Skin grafts require intimate contact with the vascularized wound bed for plasmatic imbibition (days 1–2) and inosculation/revascularization (days 3–5); hematomas or seromas beneath the graft prevent revascularization, causing graft necrosis.
2. Indicated: Limb elevation above heart level decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure and reduces interstitial edema.
3. Contraindicated: Prolonged cessation of enteral feeding in a hypermetabolic burn patient exacerbates negative nitrogen balance and wound breakdown; feeds are held only for the minimum required surgical NPO window.
4. Indicated: Immobilizing the grafted extremity for the initial 3–5 days prevents shear forces that tear fragile newly forming capillary buds.
5. Non-Essential: Repeated routine arterial blood gases are unwarranted in a non-intubated client with normal pulmonary function.
6. Contraindicated: Leaving open burns exposed to non-sterile hospital air causes desiccation and invites bacterial colonization.

question.stem:
The nurse conducts discharge teaching and evaluates Karen's understanding of long-term burn rehabilitation, scar remodeling, and skin care.

Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
question.preamble: Discharge rehabilitation planning on Post-Burn Day 21. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1100 (Post-Burn Day 21).
question.explanation:
1. Sebaceous Gland Loss: Deep partial- and full-thickness burns destroy the epidermal appendages located in the dermis, including sebaceous glands (which secrete lubricating sebum) and eccrine sweat glands (which regulate heat). Healed and grafted skin is perpetually dry, pruritic, and susceptible to cracking, requiring daily lifelong application of bland emollients.
2. Compression Garments: Hypertrophic scars occur when myofibroblasts and disordered collagen bundles proliferate excessively during the remodeling phase. Custom-fitted pressure garments (20–30 mm Hg) worn 23 hours/day for 12–18 months flatten collagen fibers, suppress vascularity, relieve itching, and prevent contractures.
3. Sun Protection: Newly healed burns and split-thickness grafts have diminished or absent melanocytes and thin epidermis. Exposure to UV rays causes severe sunburn and permanent hyperpigmentation; complete photoprotection (SPF 50+, physical covering) is essential for at least 1 year.

Right foot is pale and noticeably cooler than left foot. Capillary refill in right great toe is sluggish at 4–5 seconds. Palpation of the dorsalis pedis pulse is absent; Doppler probe reveals faint, monophasic signal. Calf is hard and unyielding. Burn surgeon immediately alerted for emergency bedside escharotomy.

1620:Burn surgeon arrives at bedside. Right calf compartment pressure measured with Stryker needle: 38 mm Hg (abnormally elevated; normal < 10–15 mm Hg; > 30 mm Hg diagnostic of compartment syndrome). Right dorsalis pedis Doppler signal has completely ceased. Immediate bedside escharotomy performed under sterile conditions: longitudinal medial and lateral incisions made through the rigid, insensate eschar of the right lower leg down to subcutaneous fat. Upon incision, the eschar edges immediately gape open by 1.5 cm with visible decompression of underlying tissues. Bleeding controlled with electrocautery. Within 5 minutes, Doppler acoustic signal returns strongly in dorsalis pedis artery; toes become warm with capillary refill < 2 seconds. Pain on passive stretch diminishes. Sterile non-adherent dressings applied.

1000 (Post-Burn Day 3):Karen is resting in the burn step-down unit. Right leg escharotomy wounds show clean subcutaneous margins with healthy granulation tissue and strong palpable pedal pulses (+2). Right forearm deep partial-thickness burns being cleansed with chlorhexidine and dressed with silver sulfadiazine cream. Enteral nutrition infusing via small-bore nasojejunal tube at 75 mL/hr (target 2,400 kcal/day, 130 g protein/day) with good tolerance and no abdominal distension. Resting energy expenditure is elevated by 60% above predicted basal rate. Serum prealbumin is 110 mg/L (target > 180 mg/L, reflecting ongoing catabolism). Blood glucose maintained between 7.0–10.0 mmol/L on sliding-scale insulin.

1330:Physical and occupational therapy assessment completed. Right ankle splinted in neutral 90-degree dorsiflexion with a multipodus boot to prevent Achilles tendon contracture and foot drop. Right knee maintained in full extension; pillows under knees removed and contraindicated. Range of motion exercises performed on right toes, knee, and shoulder following IV hydromorphone pre-medication. Topical silver sulfadiazine applied to right lower leg and forearm under sterile stretch gauze wrap. Karen actively engaged in bedside therapy.

1600 (Post-Op Day 1 / Post-Burn Day 8):Karen transferred from PACU. Meshed split-thickness autografts placed on right lower leg and right forearm; donor site on left thigh dressed with calcium alginate and semi-permeable film. Right lower extremity immobilized in posterior splint and elevated on foam ramp above heart level. Pedal pulses +2 bilaterally with warm, pink toes. Enteral nutrition resumed at goal rate (75 mL/hr). Pain controlled via PCA pump.

1100 (Post-Burn Day 21):Discharge consultation completed. Skin grafts on right leg and forearm show > 95% take, clean, intact, with resolving epithelialization. Donor site on left thigh completely healed. Custom Jobst pressure gradient garments fitted for right arm and leg; Karen demonstrates ability to don and doff garments with family assistance. Emollient skin care (plain cocoa butter / white petrolatum lotion) reviewed. Karen verbalizes understanding to wear pressure garments 23 hours daily for the next year and protect all healed skin from sun exposure. Outpatient burn therapy and clinic follow-up scheduled.

tabs.title: Burn Classification Reference
tabs.content:
American Burn Association Depth Classification:
  • 1st Degree: Epidermis only; red, dry, painful, no blisters.
  • 2nd Degree (Superficial Partial): Papillary dermis; blisters, moist, weeping, very painful.
  • 2nd Degree (Deep Partial): Reticular dermis; waxy-white mottled, less painful, sluggish blanch.
  • 3rd Degree (Full Thickness): Subcutaneous involvement; dry, leathery, charred, insensate, no blanching.
  • 4th Degree: Muscle, tendon, bone involvement; requires amputation or extensive flap coverage.

tabs.title: Wound Healing Stages Reference
tabs.content:
Four Phases of Natural Wound Healing in Burns:
  • Phase 1: Hemostasis: Platelet aggregation, fibrin clot formation, provisional matrix.
  • Phase 2: Inflammation: Neutrophil and macrophage infiltration, cytokine release (VEGF, TGF-β, PDGF), clearing debris/bacteria.
  • Phase 3: Proliferation: Fibroblast migration, collagen deposition, angiogenesis, epithelialization.
  • Phase 4: Remodeling: Collagen cross-linking, matrix remodeling by MMPs, scar contracture maturation.
